opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think people sometimes assume that because I spend so much time on risks, I must be kind of a pessimist about AI, or that I think it would be better if it never got built. That's really not how I see it.

I think the potential upside of AI is enormous, possibly bigger than anything else that's happened in history. If you get AI systems that can do the kind of work that scientists and engineers do, and do it faster and at much greater scale, you could compress decades or even centuries of progress into a much shorter period. That could mean curing diseases that have plagued people forever, dramatically reducing poverty, giving people far more abundance and freedom. When I think about what a good future could look like, a lot of it runs through advanced AI going well.

But that's kind of the point. The upside and the risk come from the same place. What makes AI so potentially beneficial is that it could be extraordinarily powerful and transformative, and that same power is what makes it dangerous if it goes wrong. That could be misaligned systems pursuing goals we didn't intend, or humans using AI to concentrate power in really unhealthy ways, or simply a transition happening so fast that our institutions can't keep up.

So I don't think of myself as anti-AI. I think of it more like this: there's a huge prize on the table, and the main thing that could cause us to miss it, or end up somewhere much worse, is handling the transition badly. Reducing those risks is how you get the benefits. I'd also say that, at the margin, the benefits don't need that much help. There are massive commercial incentives pushing AI development forward, and lots of talented people working on capabilities. The risk side is much more neglected relative to its importance, so that's where I think someone like me can add the most value.

There's also a sort of asymmetry I keep coming back to. If we're a bit more careful and slow some things down, we probably still get most of the benefits, maybe a little later. If we get it badly wrong, some of those mistakes might not be reversible. So even as someone who's genuinely excited about what AI could do, that asymmetry pushes me toward focusing on getting it right rather than getting it fast.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is something I probably don't emphasize enough, because so much of my work is about what could go wrong. But I actually think the upside here is enormous, and it's a big part of why I care about getting this right.

The way I think about it is that for most of human history, the thing that drove progress was basically the number of people doing science and innovation, and how well they could build on each other's work. If AI can do that kind of work, you could get something like a lot more scientific and technological progress in a decade than we'd otherwise get in a century. And that translates into things that matter a huge amount: cures for diseases that kill millions of people every year, massive reductions in poverty, clean energy that's cheap enough to actually displace fossil fuels, and probably a lot of things we can't even anticipate right now.

So when I think about the risks, I'm not coming from a place of wishing this technology didn't exist. I'm coming from a place of thinking the stakes are very high in both directions. If we handle it badly, we could lose a lot, maybe everything. If we handle it well, we could end up in a world that's dramatically better than today's. Those two things are really connected for me. The reason the risks are worth worrying so much about is partly that the prize is so big.

I'd also say that focusing on risk isn't really about slowing things down for the sake of it. It's more like: there are some mistakes you can recover from and some you can't. I want us to get the benefits, and I think the best way to actually get them is to avoid the catastrophic, irreversible failures along the way. So I see the two as pretty complementary, even if my day-to-day work ends up looking a lot more like worrying than celebrating.

astra-6.text:
I think the benefits could be enormous, and that’s a big part of why I care about getting this right. A lot of the things we want—better medicine, less poverty, a better understanding of the world—are held back by how much intellectual work humans can do. If AI lets us do much more of that work, it could dramatically accelerate progress.

But I don’t think that automatically means things go well. A technology that gives us that much power also creates a very serious challenge: making sure we can understand it, control it, and use it in ways that actually benefit people.

So I don’t see working on the risks as being opposed to the benefits. The upside is part of what’s at stake. I’d like us to get to a world where we can enjoy those benefits, and I think being willing to take precautions—even when they’re costly—is a pretty reasonable part of getting there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the benefits could be enormous. A lot of my interest in AI comes from the possibility that it could help us solve problems that have been extremely hard to solve: curing diseases, reducing poverty, understanding the world better. If we could automate a lot of the work that goes into scientific and technological progress, that could be a very big deal.

And I don’t think that’s in tension with being very focused on the risks. The way I think about it is: there could be an extraordinary future here, and we should be willing to do a lot of work to make sure we actually get there. Being excited about the destination doesn’t mean you should be indifferent to how you make the trip.

So my focus on risk isn’t a judgment that the benefits are small. It’s more a judgment about where additional attention and effort seem most needed. There are already very strong incentives to build more capable AI. I’m less confident that we have equally strong incentives to make sure the transition goes well for everyone.
